The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Model

Ivan Jacob Agaloos Pesigan

2026-11-03

Source: vignettes/ou.Rmd
ou.Rmd

Overview

The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) model is a continuous-time model for variables that are pulled back toward an equilibrium level after they are pushed away from it, for example, mood returning to a person’s usual level after a stressful event. Continuous time means the model describes change at every moment, not only at the occasions we measure, so the same parameters apply whether measurements are one hour or one day apart, and the spacing can differ between occasions.

The model is a state space model with two parts: a measurement model that links the observed variables to the latent (unobserved) states, and a dynamic model, here a stochastic differential equation, that describes how the latent states change over time.

This tutorial does three things:

  1. It writes the multivariate OU model as a state space model.
  2. It simulates data from the model with SimSSMOUFixed(), with every individual sharing the same parameters.
  3. It fits the model to the simulated data with the dynr and OpenMx packages and compares both sets of estimates with the values used to simulate the data.

No prior knowledge of state space models is needed. The vignettes on the vector autoregressive model and the state space model cover the discrete-time versions.

Model

The measurement model is given by \mathbf{y}_{i, t} = \boldsymbol{\nu} + \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \boldsymbol{\eta}_{i, t} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{i, t}, \quad \mathrm{with} \quad \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{i, t} \sim \mathcal{N} \left( \mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Theta} \right) where \mathbf{y}_{i, t}, \boldsymbol{\eta}_{i, t}, and \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{i, t} are random variables and \boldsymbol{\nu}, \boldsymbol{\Lambda}, and \boldsymbol{\Theta} are model parameters. \mathbf{y}_{i, t} represents a vector of observed random variables, \boldsymbol{\eta}_{i, t} a vector of latent random variables, and \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{i, t} a vector of random measurement errors, at time t and individual i. \boldsymbol{\nu} denotes a vector of intercepts, \boldsymbol{\Lambda} a matrix of factor loadings, and \boldsymbol{\Theta} the covariance matrix of \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}.

In words, each observed variable is an intercept plus a weighted combination of the latent variables plus measurement error. The latent variables \boldsymbol{\eta}_{i, t} are the quantities we care about (for example, a person’s true stress level), and the observed variables \mathbf{y}_{i, t} are noisy measurements of them. Separating measurement error from true change is the main reason to use a state space model: measurement error affects only the occasion it occurs on, while changes in the latent variables carry over in time.

An alternative representation of the measurement error is given by \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{i, t} = \boldsymbol{\Theta}^{\frac{1}{2}} \mathbf{z}_{i, t}, \quad \mathrm{with} \quad \mathbf{z}_{i, t} \sim \mathcal{N} \left( \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I} \right) where \mathbf{z}_{i, t} is a vector of independent standard normal random variables and \left( \boldsymbol{\Theta}^{\frac{1}{2}} \right) \left( \boldsymbol{\Theta}^{\frac{1}{2}} \right)^{\prime} = \boldsymbol{\Theta} .

The dynamic structure is given by \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\eta}_{i, t} = \boldsymbol{\Phi} \left( \boldsymbol{\eta}_{i, t} - \boldsymbol{\mu} \right) \mathrm{d}t + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{\frac{1}{2}} \mathrm{d} \mathbf{W}_{i, t} where \boldsymbol{\mu} is the long-term mean or equilibrium level, \boldsymbol{\Phi} is the rate of mean reversion, determining how quickly the variable returns to its mean, \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is the matrix of volatility or randomness in the process, and \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{W} is a Wiener process or Brownian motion, which represents random fluctuations.

In words, \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\eta}_{i, t} is the change in the latent variables over a very short time \mathrm{d}t. The change has two parts: a pull toward the equilibrium \boldsymbol{\mu}, proportional to the distance \boldsymbol{\eta}_{i, t} - \boldsymbol{\mu}, and random fluctuations with covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} per unit time.

  • With this sign convention, a diagonal element \phi_{jj} is negative for a variable that returns to its equilibrium. The more negative it is, the faster the return.
  • An off-diagonal element \phi_{jk} is the effect of the distance of variable k from its equilibrium on the rate of change of variable j. As in the discrete-time models, the row is the outcome and the column is the predictor.

For the process to settle around \boldsymbol{\mu}, all eigenvalues of \boldsymbol{\Phi} must have negative real parts.

Over a time interval \Delta t, the OU model implies a discrete-time vector autoregressive model with transition matrix \boldsymbol{\beta} = \exp \left( \boldsymbol{\Phi} \Delta t \right), the matrix exponential. SimSSMOUFixed() uses this exact discretization to simulate the data, so no approximation error is introduced.

Diagram

State space diagram of the OU model.

The model in state space form, at the first three occasions of measurement, \Delta t apart (t = 0, \Delta t, 2 \Delta t), with every element of the state drawn. Squares are observed variables and circles are latent variables. Each latent variable \eta_{j, t} has one indicator Y_{j, t} with a loading of 1, and measurement error \varepsilon_{j, t} with variance \theta_{jj}. The arrows between occasions are the elements of \boldsymbol{\beta} = \exp \left( \boldsymbol{\Phi} \Delta t \right). Because \boldsymbol{\Phi} is lower triangular in this example, so is \boldsymbol{\beta}: \eta_{1} affects \eta_{2} and \eta_{3}, and \eta_{2} affects \eta_{3}. \zeta_{j, t} is the process noise from t = \Delta t on. Its covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Psi} follows from \boldsymbol{\Phi}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, and \Delta t and is full, so the process noise terms covary (the gray arrows \psi_{jk}). A loop on a variable is its variance and a curved two-headed arrow a covariance. At t = 0, the initial condition \boldsymbol{\eta}_{0} \sim \mathcal{N} \left( \boldsymbol{\mu}_{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0} \right) gives the variances \sigma_{jj} and covariances \sigma_{jk} of the latent variables. The exact discretization gives \boldsymbol{\beta} and \boldsymbol{\Psi} from \boldsymbol{\Phi}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, and \Delta t; \boldsymbol{\Lambda} maps the state to the observed variables, and \boldsymbol{\Theta} is the covariance matrix of the measurement error. SimSSMOUFixed() takes phi, lambda, delta_t, mu0, and the Cholesky factors of \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \boldsymbol{\Theta}, and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0} (sigma_l, theta_l, and sigma0_l), and does the discretization itself.

Data Generation

Notation

Let t = 1000 be the number of time points and n = 100 be the number of individuals.

Let the measurement model intercept vector \boldsymbol{\nu} be given by

\boldsymbol{\nu} = \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ \end{array} \right) .

Let the factor loadings matrix \boldsymbol{\Lambda} be given by

\boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \left( \begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{array} \right) .

Let the measurement error covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Theta} be given by

\boldsymbol{\Theta} = \left( \begin{array}{ccc} 0.2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.2 \\ \end{array} \right) .

With \boldsymbol{\nu} = \mathbf{0} and \boldsymbol{\Lambda} = \mathbf{I}, each observed variable measures one latent variable, and \boldsymbol{\Theta} adds measurement error with variance 0.2 to each.

Let the initial condition \boldsymbol{\eta}_{0} be given by

\boldsymbol{\eta}_{0} \sim \mathcal{N} \left( \boldsymbol{\mu}_{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0} \right)

\boldsymbol{\mu}_{0} = \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ \end{array} \right)

\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0} = \left( \begin{array}{ccc} 0.3425148 & 0.3296023 & 0.0343817 \\ 0.3296023 & 0.5664625 & 0.2545955 \\ 0.0343817 & 0.2545955 & 0.2999909 \\ \end{array} \right) .

Let the long-term mean vector \boldsymbol{\mu} be given by

\boldsymbol{\mu} = \left( \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ \end{array} \right) .

Let the rate of mean reversion matrix \boldsymbol{\Phi} be given by

\boldsymbol{\Phi} = \left( \begin{array}{ccc} -0.357 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.771 & -0.511 & 0 \\ -0.45 & 0.729 & -0.693 \\ \end{array} \right) .

Read the columns as predictors and the rows as outcomes. The diagonal elements are all negative, so each variable returns to its equilibrium. In addition, \eta_{1} pushes up the change in \eta_{2} (0.771), \eta_{2} pushes up the change in \eta_{3} (0.729), and \eta_{1} pushes down the change in \eta_{3} (-0.45). Because \boldsymbol{\Phi} is lower triangular, its eigenvalues are its diagonal elements, all negative, so the process is stable.

Let the dynamic process noise covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} be given by

\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \left( \begin{array}{ccc} 0.2445556 & 0.0220159 & -0.0500476 \\ 0.0220159 & 0.070678 & 0.0153946 \\ -0.0500476 & 0.0153946 & 0.0755306 \\ \end{array} \right) .

Let \Delta t = 0.1.

The data are measured every 0.1 time units. For example, if the time unit is one day, the 1000 occasions span 99.9 days.

The initial condition describes where each individual starts. Here, the mean vector and covariance matrix of \boldsymbol{\eta}_{0} are the model-implied mean and covariance of the stable process, computed with LinSDEMeanEta() and LinSDECovEta(), so the data are stationary from the first time point.

Visualizing the Dynamics Without Measurement Error and Process Noise (n = 5 with Different Initial Condition)

To see what \boldsymbol{\Phi} alone does, we first simulate five individuals with the process noise and the measurement error set to zero. Each individual starts at a different point, and the trajectories return to the equilibrium at a speed set by \boldsymbol{\Phi}.

Using the SimSSMOUFixed Function from the simStateSpace Package to Simulate Data

Now we add the process noise and the measurement error and simulate the full data set. as.data.frame() returns the data in long format, one row per individual and time point, with the columns id, time, y1, y2, and y3. The time column holds the actual measurement times (0, 0.1, 0.2, and so on), which the continuous-time model uses.

library(simStateSpace)
sim <- SimSSMOUFixed(
  n = n,
  time = time,
  delta_t = delta_t,
  mu0 = mu0,
  sigma0_l = sigma0_l,
  mu = mu,
  phi = phi,
  sigma_l = sigma_l,
  nu = nu,
  lambda = lambda,
  theta_l = theta_l,
  type = 0
)
data <- as.data.frame(sim)
head(data)
#>   id time          y1         y2         y3

Model Fitting

The same simulated data are fitted with two programs that estimate state space models by maximum likelihood with the Kalman filter: dynr and OpenMx. The section Population Values and Estimates compares their estimates with the population values.

dynr

We fit the model with dynr, which estimates state space models by maximum likelihood. For continuous-time models, dynr uses the time between measurements to get the implied discrete-time model for each interval, then applies the Kalman filter.

A dynr model is built from pieces that match the equations above: the data, the initial condition, the measurement model, the dynamic model, and the noise. Each parameter gets a name (for example, phi_2_1 for \phi_{21}`), and the same name used in two places means one shared parameter. The starting values are set to the population values for convenience; with real data, they would be rough guesses.

Prepare Data

Tell dynr which columns hold the individual, the time, and the observed variables.

dynr_data <- dynr::dynr.data(
  dataframe = data,
  id = "id",
  time = "time",
  observed = c("y1", "y2", "y3")
)

Prepare Initial Condition

The mean \boldsymbol{\mu}_{0} and covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0} of the initial state are estimated. The covariance matrix is symmetric, so sigma0_2_1 appears both above and below the diagonal.

dynr_initial <- dynr::prep.initial(
  values.inistate = mu0,
  params.inistate = c("mu0_1_1", "mu0_2_1", "mu0_3_1"),
  values.inicov = sigma0,
  params.inicov = matrix(
    data = c(
      "sigma0_1_1", "sigma0_2_1", "sigma0_3_1",
      "sigma0_2_1", "sigma0_2_2", "sigma0_3_2",
      "sigma0_3_1", "sigma0_3_2", "sigma0_3_3"
    ),
    nrow = 3
  )
)

Prepare Measurement Model

The loadings \boldsymbol{\Lambda} are an identity matrix with no free parameters ("fixed").

dynr_measurement <- dynr::prep.measurement(
  values.load = diag(3),
  params.load = matrix(data = "fixed", nrow = 3, ncol = 3),
  state.names = c("eta_1", "eta_2", "eta_3"),
  obs.names = c("y1", "y2", "y3")
)

Prepare Dynamic Process

Each formula is the rate of change of one latent variable: the effects \phi_{jk} of the distances of the three latent variables from their equilibria \mu_{k}. isContinuousTime = TRUE makes this a continuous-time model.

dynr_dynamics <- dynr::prep.formulaDynamics(
  formula = list(  
    eta_1 ~ (phi_1_1 * (eta_1 - mu_1_1)) + (phi_1_2 * (eta_2 - mu_2_1)) + (phi_1_3 * (eta_3 - mu_3_1)),
    eta_2 ~ (phi_2_1 * (eta_1 - mu_1_1)) + (phi_2_2 * (eta_2 - mu_2_1)) + (phi_2_3 * (eta_3 - mu_3_1)),
    eta_3 ~ (phi_3_1 * (eta_1 - mu_1_1)) + (phi_3_2 * (eta_2 - mu_2_1)) + (phi_3_3 * (eta_3 - mu_3_1))
  ),
  startval = c(
    mu_1_1 = mu[1], mu_2_1 = mu[2], mu_3_1 = mu[3],
    phi_1_1 = phi[1, 1], phi_1_2 = phi[1, 2], phi_1_3 = phi[1, 3],
    phi_2_1 = phi[2, 1], phi_2_2 = phi[2, 2], phi_2_3 = phi[2, 3],
    phi_3_1 = phi[3, 1], phi_3_2 = phi[3, 2], phi_3_3 = phi[3, 3]
  ),
  isContinuousTime = TRUE
)

Prepare Process Noise

The diffusion covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} is estimated in full. The measurement error covariance \boldsymbol{\Theta} is diagonal: the three error variances are estimated, and the error covariances are fixed at zero.

dynr_noise <- dynr::prep.noise(
  values.latent = sigma,
  params.latent = matrix(
    data = c(
      "sigma_1_1", "sigma_2_1", "sigma_3_1",
      "sigma_2_1", "sigma_2_2", "sigma_3_2",
      "sigma_3_1", "sigma_3_2", "sigma_3_3"
    ),
    nrow = 3
  ),
  values.observed = theta,
  params.observed = matrix(
    data = c(
      "theta_1_1", "fixed", "fixed",
      "fixed", "theta_2_2", "fixed",
      "fixed", "fixed", "theta_3_3"
    ),
    nrow = 3
  )
)

Prepare the Model

The pieces are put together into one model. dynr writes the model as C code to outfile and compiles it.

model <- dynr::dynr.model(
  data = dynr_data,
  initial = dynr_initial,
  measurement = dynr_measurement,
  dynamics = dynr_dynamics,
  noise = dynr_noise,
  outfile = "ou.c"
)

Add lower and upper bounds on the elements of \boldsymbol{\Phi} to keep the optimizer away from implausible values.

model$lb[
  c(
    "phi_1_1",
    "phi_1_2",
    "phi_1_3",
    "phi_2_1",
    "phi_2_2",
    "phi_2_3",
    "phi_3_1",
    "phi_3_2",
    "phi_3_3"
  )
] <- -1.5
model$ub[
  c(
    "phi_1_1",
    "phi_1_2",
    "phi_1_3",
    "phi_2_1",
    "phi_2_2",
    "phi_2_3",
    "phi_3_1",
    "phi_3_2",
    "phi_3_3"
  )
] <- +1.5

The plot below shows the model equations with the parameter names.

Fit the Model 

results <- dynr::dynr.cook(
  model,
  debug_flag = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)

OpenMx: State Space Model

OpenMx (Neale et al., 2016) fits the same state space model with its own Kalman filter (OpenMx::mxExpectationStateSpace(); Hunter (2018)). Its matrices have the names used in engineering: A is the transition matrix \boldsymbol{\beta}, B holds the intercepts of the dynamic model, C is the loading matrix \boldsymbol{\Lambda}, D holds the intercepts of the measurement model, Q is the process noise covariance matrix, and R is the measurement error covariance matrix. The parameter labels are the dynr names; as in dynr, a label used in two places is one shared parameter, and the starting values are the population values.

Two details differ from dynr. First, OpenMx reads the data as a single time series. To start the filter again at the first occasion of every individual, each individual gets a group, and all groups use the matrices of one parent model, so every individual has the same parameters. Second, OpenMx starts the filter one occasion before the first row, so the first row has the state mean \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}_{0} + \mathbf{B} \mathbf{u} and the state covariance \mathbf{A} \mathbf{P}_{0} \mathbf{A}^{\prime} + \mathbf{Q}, with the constant input \mathbf{u} = 1. Setting \mathbf{x}_{0} = \mathbf{A}^{-1} \left( \boldsymbol{\mu}_{0} - \mathbf{B} \mathbf{u} \right) and \mathbf{P}_{0} = \mathbf{A}^{-1} \left( \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0} - \mathbf{Q} \right) \left( \mathbf{A}^{-1} \right)^{\prime} gives the first occasion the initial condition of the model, so the likelihood is the same as in dynr. This needs an invertible \mathbf{A}, which holds here.

The two helper functions below are the same in every vignette of the package. MxMat() makes an OpenMx matrix from values and dynr-style labels ("fixed" marks a fixed element), and FitMxSSM() builds the groups and fits the model.

MxMat <- function(values, labels, name) {
  values <- as.matrix(values)
  labels <- matrix(
    data = labels,
    nrow = nrow(values),
    ncol = ncol(values)
  )
  free <- labels != "fixed"
  labels[!free] <- NA
  OpenMx::mxMatrix(
    type = "Full",
    values = values,
    free = free,
    labels = labels,
    name = name
  )
}
FitMxSSM <- function(data, observed, matrices, name) {
  # the groups refer to the matrices of the parent model
  shared <- function(x) {
    paste0(name, ".", x)
  }
  expectation <- OpenMx::mxExpectationStateSpace(
    A = shared("A"),
    B = shared("B"),
    C = shared("C"),
    D = shared("D"),
    Q = shared("Q"),
    R = shared("R"),
    x0 = shared("x0"),
    P0 = shared("P0"),
    u = shared("u")
  )
  # OpenMx needs the names of the observed variables and of the states on C
  for (i in seq_along(matrices)) {
    if (matrices[[i]]$name == "C") {
      dimnames(matrices[[i]]) <- list(
        observed,
        paste0("eta_", seq_len(ncol(matrices[[i]]$values)))
      )
    }
  }
  persons <- split(
    x = data[, observed, drop = FALSE],
    f = data[, "id"]
  )
  groups <- paste0("id_", names(persons))
  submodels <- lapply(
    X = seq_along(persons),
    FUN = function(i) {
      OpenMx::mxModel(
        name = groups[i],
        expectation,
        OpenMx::mxFitFunctionML(),
        OpenMx::mxData(
          observed = persons[[i]],
          type = "raw"
        )
      )
    }
  )
  model <- OpenMx::mxModel(
    name = name,
    matrices,
    OpenMx::mxMatrix(
      type = "Unit",
      nrow = 1,
      ncol = 1,
      name = "u"
    ),
    # the first occasion gets the initial condition of the model
    OpenMx::mxAlgebra(
      expression = solve(A) %*% (mu0 - B %*% u),
      name = "x0"
    ),
    OpenMx::mxAlgebra(
      expression = solve(A) %*% (sigma0 - Q) %*% t(solve(A)),
      name = "P0"
    ),
    submodels,
    OpenMx::mxFitFunctionMultigroup(groups = groups)
  )
  # retries from perturbed starting values only if the first run fails
  OpenMx::mxTryHard(
    model = model,
    extraTries = 5,
    silent = TRUE
  )
}

The model is in continuous time, so the discrete-time matrices A, B, and Q are the exact discretization of the drift matrix \boldsymbol{\Phi}, the equilibrium \boldsymbol{\mu}, and the diffusion matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma} over the interval \Delta_{t}, written as OpenMx algebras: \mathbf{A} = \exp \left( \boldsymbol{\Phi} \Delta_{t} \right), \mathbf{B} = \left( \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A} \right) \boldsymbol{\mu}, and \mathbf{Q} from the matrix exponential of a block matrix (Van Loan, 1978). The free parameters are still \boldsymbol{\Phi}, \boldsymbol{\mu}, and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, with the dynr labels. We use the discrete-time expectation with these algebras rather than OpenMx::mxExpectationStateSpaceContinuousTime(): in our checks with OpenMx 2.22.11, its process noise covariance over an interval did not match the exact one when \boldsymbol{\Phi} is not symmetric. The matrix exponential omxExponential() in the algebras is also evaluated in R, so OpenMx is attached.

library(OpenMx)
#> To take full advantage of multiple cores, use:
#>   mxOption(key='Number of Threads', value=parallel::detectCores()) #now
#>   Sys.setenv(OMP_NUM_THREADS=parallel::detectCores()) #before library(OpenMx)
labels_phi <- matrix(
  data = c(
    "phi_1_1", "phi_2_1", "phi_3_1",
    "phi_1_2", "phi_2_2", "phi_3_2",
    "phi_1_3", "phi_2_3", "phi_3_3"
  ),
  nrow = 3
)
labels_sigma <- matrix(
  data = c(
    "sigma_1_1", "sigma_2_1", "sigma_3_1",
    "sigma_2_1", "sigma_2_2", "sigma_3_2",
    "sigma_3_1", "sigma_3_2", "sigma_3_3"
  ),
  nrow = 3
)
labels_theta <- matrix(
  data = c(
    "theta_1_1", "fixed", "fixed",
    "fixed", "theta_2_2", "fixed",
    "fixed", "fixed", "theta_3_3"
  ),
  nrow = 3
)
labels_sigma0 <- matrix(
  data = c(
    "sigma0_1_1", "sigma0_2_1", "sigma0_3_1",
    "sigma0_2_1", "sigma0_2_2", "sigma0_3_2",
    "sigma0_3_1", "sigma0_3_2", "sigma0_3_3"
  ),
  nrow = 3
)
mx_matrices <- list(
  MxMat(values = phi, labels = labels_phi, name = "phi"),
  MxMat(
    values = mu,
    labels = c("mu_1_1", "mu_2_1", "mu_3_1"),
    name = "mu"
  ),
  MxMat(values = sigma, labels = labels_sigma, name = "sigma"),
  MxMat(values = delta_t, labels = "fixed", name = "delta_t"),
  MxMat(values = diag(3), labels = "fixed", name = "I"),
  MxMat(
    values = matrix(data = 0, nrow = 3, ncol = 3),
    labels = "fixed",
    name = "Z"
  ),
  # exact discretization over delta_t
  OpenMx::mxAlgebra(
    expression = omxExponential(phi * delta_t),
    name = "A"
  ),
  OpenMx::mxAlgebra(
    expression = (I - A) %*% mu,
    name = "B"
  ),
  OpenMx::mxAlgebra(
    expression = omxExponential(
      rbind(cbind(-phi, sigma), cbind(Z, t(phi))) * delta_t
    ),
    name = "vanloan"
  ),
  OpenMx::mxAlgebra(
    expression = t(vanloan[4:6, 4:6]) %*% vanloan[1:3, 4:6],
    name = "Q"
  ),
  MxMat(values = lambda, labels = "fixed", name = "C"),
  MxMat(values = nu, labels = "fixed", name = "D"),
  MxMat(values = theta, labels = labels_theta, name = "R"),
  MxMat(
    values = mu0,
    labels = c("mu0_1_1", "mu0_2_1", "mu0_3_1"),
    name = "mu0"
  ),
  MxMat(values = sigma0, labels = labels_sigma0, name = "sigma0")
)
fit_mx_ssm <- FitMxSSM(
  data = data,
  observed = c("y1", "y2", "y3"),
  matrices = mx_matrices,
  name = "ou"
)

Population Values and Estimates

Each table below puts the population values used to simulate the data next to the estimates of one method. Bias is the estimate minus the population value. Because each model is fitted to a single simulated data set, this is the error of one estimate, not a Monte Carlo bias, which would average over many replications. The 95% confidence interval is the Wald interval, \hat{\theta} \pm 1.96 \times \mathrm{SE}, unless the caption says otherwise, and Covers shows whether it contains the population value. The parameter names are the dynr names in every table.

EstimatesTable <- function(population, estimate, se, ll = NULL, ul = NULL) {
  z <- stats::qnorm(p = 0.975)
  if (is.null(ll)) {
    ll <- estimate - z * se
  }
  if (is.null(ul)) {
    ul <- estimate + z * se
  }
  data.frame(
    Parameter = names(population),
    Population = unname(population),
    Estimate = unname(estimate),
    SE = unname(se),
    Bias = unname(estimate - population),
    `2.5%` = unname(ll),
    `97.5%` = unname(ul),
    Covers = unname(population >= ll & population <= ul),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}
# the population value for each dynr parameter name,
# for example, "beta_1_2" is beta[1, 2] and "mu0_2_1" is mu0[2]
population <- vapply(
  X = strsplit(x = names(coef(results)), split = "_"),
  FUN = function(x) {
    as.matrix(get(x[1]))[as.integer(x[2]), as.integer(x[3])]
  },
  FUN.VALUE = numeric(1)
)
names(population) <- names(coef(results))

dynr 

dynr_est <- coef(results)
dynr_se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(results)))
knitr::kable(
  x = EstimatesTable(
    population = population,
    estimate = dynr_est[names(population)],
    se = dynr_se[names(population)]
  ),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Population values and dynr estimates (one simulated data set)"
)
